new.definition: A hot, tomato based Louisiana stew more than a sauce, usually begun on a roux with onion, celery and bell pepper, then simmered with tomatoes and pepper until thick. It smothers whatever the cook has, chicken, rabbit, turtle, alligator or shrimp, and it is served over rice. The name is French for a sharp, pricking taste. In a French kitchen sauce piquante is a different thing: a brown sauce sharpened with vinegar, shallots and chopped gherkins.
new.guest: Sauce piquante is a Cajun country classic: meat or seafood simmered in a peppery tomato gravy built on a roux with onion, celery and bell pepper, and served over rice. Piquante means sharp, so it carries some heat. On our Thanksgiving menu it was shrimp in a Creole tomato gravy over popcorn rice pilaf, finished with pickled peppers.
new.kitchen: Built like a stew: the roux, then the onion, celery and bell pepper, then tomato and stock, simmered until it thickens. How dark the roux goes, how hot the pepper runs and when the shrimp go in are the chef’s calls, so ask at lineup before you promise a guest the heat.
new.compare: Shrimp Creole is its nearest neighbor: both are shrimp in a tomato sauce over rice, but a sauce piquante is usually started on a roux and runs hotter. Étouffée, the other cousin, is a roux gravy with little or no tomato.

new.background: Piquant comes from the French verb piquer, to prick or sting, and in English it names a sharp, biting taste. In classical French cooking sauce piquante is one of the brown sauces: a reduction of shallots, white wine and vinegar finished with brown veal stock, chopped gherkins and herbs, the version Auguste Escoffier (1846 to 1935) set down. The Picayune’s Creole Cook Book, first published in New Orleans in 1901, printed a Piquant Sauce among its sauces. In Cajun country the name came to mean something heartier. Cajun and Creole cooks use it for a hot, tomato based sauce that smothers meat and rice, a stew begun on a roux and the holy trinity and cooked with chicken, rabbit, turtle, alligator or seafood. When or where the Louisiana dish first took the French name, no record shows.

new.definition: A Southern gravy of fat and flour cooked into a roux, then simmered with tomatoes and a little broth, milk or water until thick and savory. Bacon drippings are the old fat and butter the common stand in, and many cooks add a pinch of sugar to soften the acid. The roux is what makes it a gravy and not a plain tomato sauce. On the Thanksgiving Day menu a Creole tomato gravy was the sauce of the Shrimp Sauce Piquante.
new.guest: Tomato gravy is a Southern classic: a roux of flour and fat simmered with tomatoes into a thick, savory sauce, rounder and richer than a plain tomato sauce. On our Thanksgiving shrimp sauce piquante it was a Creole tomato gravy, warm and peppery, over the rice.
new.kitchen: The flour cooks in the fat until it starts to color, then the tomatoes and liquid go in and it simmers until it coats a spoon, tasted for acid along the way. What went into the house Creole tomato gravy, and how hot it ran, was the kitchen’s to say.
new.compare: New Orleans red gravy is its nearest neighbor: red gravy is the slow cooked tomato sauce of the city’s Sicilian families, and most cooks make it with no roux, while a tomato gravy is always thickened with one. The roux is the tell.

new.background: Tomato gravy belongs to the Southern home kitchen and to thrift: a spoon of flour in the bacon drippings, then tomatoes, fresh from the garden in summer or from the jars put up for winter, a quick fix one food writer calls a reminder of the summer garden. In southern Appalachia it is a breakfast gravy over biscuits, and Saveur notes it as a partner for biscuits in parts of Mississippi, Alabama and Florida. New Orleans has a tomato gravy story of its own. Sicilian immigrants came through the port in great numbers from about 1885 to 1915, and their slow cooked tomato sauce became the city’s red gravy, a name that set it apart from the brown gravies New Orleans cooks had made for generations. Some stir a roux into it; most do not.

new.definition: A tomato grown in southeast Louisiana, traditionally in the rich alluvial soil of the river parishes below New Orleans, and left to ripen on the vine before it is picked. The name is a regional marketing term, not a variety: farmers in St. Bernard and Plaquemines Parishes first sold their tomatoes as Creole, and today the name is used for almost any red, medium to large tomato grown in Louisiana. It is a summer crop, so in late fall what goes into a dish that carries the name is the kitchen’s to say.
new.guest: A Creole tomato is a Louisiana tomato, grown in the river soil just below New Orleans and left to ripen on the vine. The name speaks to where it was grown, not to one variety. On our Thanksgiving menu the shrimp sauce piquante came in a Creole tomato gravy.
new.kitchen: In summer the kitchen can buy them local and vine ripe; out of season, ask the chef what tomatoes went into a dish that carries the Creole name before telling a guest they were local.
new.compare: The LSU Creole, a heat tolerant variety the university bred for Louisiana gardens, is its nearest namesake: that is one named cultivar, while a Creole tomato at the market is any Louisiana grown tomato sold under the regional name. Ask where it was grown, not what variety it is.

new.background: Creole began as a name farmers gave their crop, not a seed they planted. Growers in St. Bernard and Plaquemines Parishes, on the alluvial land along the Mississippi below New Orleans, sold their vine ripened tomatoes as Creole while growing several varieties under the name, and home gardeners who bought them saved the seed and passed it along. The Louisiana Department of Agriculture has never regulated the word, so it came to cover almost any red, medium to large tomato grown in the state. Around 1970 the LSU tomato breeding program released a heat tolerant variety of its own and named it Creole, with medium, deep red fruit; its yields were poor, and the university did not keep up its seed stock. The market name and the variety are two different things, and the name is about place.

new.definition: A way of cooking rice in which the dry grains are first stirred in hot fat, often with onion, then simmered in a measured amount of stock until the liquid is absorbed. The fat coats each grain and sets the starch on its surface, so the rice cooks up fluffy and separate rather than sticky. Spices, vegetables, meat or nuts can go into the pot. On the Thanksgiving Day menu a pilaf of popcorn rice sat under the Shrimp Sauce Piquante.
new.guest: A pilaf is rice toasted in butter or oil before the stock goes in, so every grain stays separate and picks up a light, toasty flavor. Under our Thanksgiving shrimp sauce piquante it was a pilaf of Louisiana popcorn rice, there to catch the tomato gravy.
new.kitchen: The aromatics soften in the fat, the rice is stirred in until it is coated and turns opaque, then hot stock goes in at a set ratio and the pot is covered and left to cook gently until the liquid is gone. What the house cooked into its popcorn rice pilaf was a question for lineup.
new.compare: Plain boiled or steamed rice is its nearest neighbor: that rice goes straight into the water, while a pilaf is toasted in fat first and cooked in stock. The toasting is the tell, and it is why the grains stay apart.

new.background: Pilaf came into English through the Turkish pilav, from the Persian polow, and Merriam-Webster dates its first known English use to 1609. In Persian the word is first attested in a fourteenth century satirical poem, Mouse and Cat, and its recipes appear in two Safavid cookbooks compiled in the 1520s and the 1590s. In Iran a polow is rice cooked with other ingredients layered into the pot, set against chelow, rice cooked on its own. The dish and its name spread widely, to India as pulao and to the Carolina coast as pilau, where enslaved West Africans and their Gullah Geechee descendants cooked it with the rice they grew. There it became perloo, a one pot dish of rice cooked in stock with shrimp or chicken, a cousin of the pilaf under a Louisiana sauce piquante.

new.definition: A New Orleans dish of large shrimp, traditionally cooked with their heads and shells on, in a pan sauce of butter, black pepper and Worcestershire, often with garlic, lemon and hot sauce. It never goes near a grill or a smoker: the barbecue in the name points to the reddish brown color of the sauce and its peppery bite. Guests peel the shrimp at the table, which makes it a messy, hands on dish.
new.guest: New Orleans BBQ shrimp is never barbecued: it is shrimp cooked in a rich pan sauce of butter, black pepper and Worcestershire, a dish born Uptown at Pascal’s Manale in the 1950s. Our Thanksgiving side carried those buttery, peppery flavors into a holiday stuffing for the table.
new.kitchen: Cooked fast in a hot pan so the shrimp stay tender, with the heads left on in the traditional version because they flavor the sauce. What the Thanksgiving stuffing was built on was the kitchen’s to say, so describe the style, not the recipe.
new.compare: Shrimp off a grill or a barbecue pit is its namesake and its opposite: those take their flavor from fire and smoke, while New Orleans BBQ shrimp never touches a grill and takes everything from its butter and pepper sauce. No fire is the tell.

new.background: Barbecue shrimp is credited to Pascal’s Manale, an Uptown New Orleans restaurant that opened as Manale’s in 1913 and was renamed Pascal’s Manale when the founder’s nephew added his own first name in tribute to his uncle. The dish arrived in the 1950s; accounts give 1953, 1954 or simply the middle of the decade. The story usually told is that a regular came back from a business trip to Chicago describing a shrimp dish he had eaten there, and the kitchen worked out its own version from his account, though no record confirms it. Other New Orleans kitchens took the dish up, each with its own sauce of butter, pepper and Worcestershire, and the traditional version keeps the shrimp heads on for flavor. There is no grill, no coals and no smoke in any of them.

deepen.background: People kept food in brine and vinegar long before anyone wrote a recipe down. Pickling is generally traced to Mesopotamia around 2400 BCE, the date the New York Food Museum gives, though its true start is unknown. In the American South, peppers steeped in vinegar became part of the table. The Virginia House-Wife, the 1824 cookbook of Mary Randolph (1762 to 1828), set down a vinegar flavored with cayenne peppers, and Colonial Williamsburg and Monticello have both published versions of it. In Louisiana, Edmund McIlhenny (1815 to 1890) grew his first commercial crop of peppers on Avery Island in 1868 for a sauce of peppers, Avery Island salt and vinegar, and the next year he sent 658 bottles to grocers around the Gulf Coast, many of them in New Orleans.
deepen.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: the pickled peppers on the Shrimp Sauce Piquante
deepen.guest: Pickled means kept in vinegar or brine, so it turns tangy and keeps its crunch. On our Thanksgiving shrimp sauce piquante, pickled peppers gave a sharp, bright bite against the warm tomato gravy.
